name: Reel
text: Adopt **Product Ops defining breach thresholds upfront** for every snapshot. This removes the gaming risk Scriv flagged—teams can’t set weak thresholds to avoid alerts—while keeping the real-time alert system sharp. The trade-off is Product Ops must invest time upfront to draft clear, objective thresholds for every risk type, but that cost is paid once and prevents downstream chaos.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk isn’t vague thresholds—it’s that Product Ops can’t define them fairly for every team without becoming the bottleneck. Instead, mandate a **cross-functional "threshold council"** (Engineering, Product, Legal, Compliance) that sets breach rules once per quarter, then Product Ops enforces them. Settle it by having the council publish the rules in a public doc and measuring how often teams game them in the next cycle.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt the rule that **Product Ops defines the breach thresholds upfront for every snapshot**, enforced at creation time. This removes the temptation for teams to game their own thresholds and ensures alerts only fire when risks truly matter. The trade-off is that Product Ops must invest time upfront to set defensible thresholds, but this beats cleaning up bad data later.

name: Sift
text: The real risk isn’t vague thresholds—it’s that Product Ops defining them upfront turns the snapshot into a bureaucratic formality. Instead, mandate that breach thresholds are co-defined by the decision owner *and* Product Ops *at the moment of the snapshot*, forcing real-time negotiation and preventing gaming. Settle it by piloting this with one high-stakes snapshot and measuring whether thresholds are ever adjusted downward in the first 30 days.
